parts.title: Course enquiry
parts.context_zh: 第一部分：一位男士打电话给社区中心，咨询陶艺课

lines.en: Good morning, Riverside Community Centre, Sarah speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I'm calling about the evening classes. I saw something about a beginners' course in pottery.
Yes, the pottery course. It starts next month, and there are still a few places left. Shall I take your details?
Yes, please.
Can I have your name?
It's David Hartley. That's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y.
lines.say: It's David Hartley. That's H. A. R. T. L. E. Y.

lines.en: Thank you, Mr Hartley. And a contact number?
My mobile's best. It's 07946 381 552.
lines.say: My mobile's best. It's oh seven nine four six, three eight one, five five two.

lines.en: Lovely. And can I ask how you heard about the course? Was it from our website?
No, I haven't looked at the website, actually. A friend mentioned it a while ago, but what made me call was an advert in the local newspaper.
Great, I'll put that down. Now, the classes run on Tuesday evenings.
Oh, really? I thought it said Thursday.
It used to be on Thursdays, but we've moved it to Tuesdays this term. Is that all right for you?
Yes, Tuesday's fine. What time does it start?
The building opens at a quarter to seven, but the class itself starts at 7.15, and it finishes at nine.
lines.say: The building opens at a quarter to seven, but the class itself starts at seven fifteen, and it finishes at nine.

lines.en: OK. And how much does the course cost?
The full price is 120 pounds for ten weeks, but there's a reduced price of 95 pounds for people who live in the area. Do you live locally?
lines.say: The full price is one hundred and twenty pounds for ten weeks, but there's a reduced price of ninety-five pounds for people who live in the area. Do you live locally?

lines.en: Yes, I'm on Mill Road, just round the corner.
Then it's the lower price for you. That includes all the clay and the cost of firing your pots in the kiln.
Do I need to bring anything? Tools, or special clothes?
The tools are provided, but it can get quite messy, so please bring an apron.
Right. And where exactly are the classes held? I've only been in the main hall before.
They're not in the main hall. They're in the Garden Room, which is at the back of the building.
And is there somewhere to park?
Our own car park is closed in the evenings, I'm afraid, but you can use the free car park behind the library. It's only two minutes' walk.
That's fine. And how do I pay? Can I pay by card when I come in?
You can pay by card online. But if you'd rather pay at reception, we only take cash, I'm afraid.
I'll come in and pay with cash, then. Thanks very much for your help.

parts.title: Volunteer induction
parts.context_zh: 第二部分：湿地保护中心的志愿者协调员给新志愿者做入职介绍

lines.en: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hartfield Wetland Centre. My name's Peter, and I'm the volunteer coordinator. Before you start your first shift, I'd like to give you a bit of background and go through a few practical things.

The centre opened in 1998 on the site of an old gravel quarry. When the digging stopped, the pits filled with water, and over the years they've become home to a huge variety of birds, insects and plants. People often assume the land was always a nature reserve, or that it used to be farmland, but in fact it was industrial land for nearly fifty years.
lines.say: The centre opened in nineteen ninety-eight on the site of an old gravel quarry. When the digging stopped, the pits filled with water, and over the years they've become home to a huge variety of birds, insects and plants. People often assume the land was always a nature reserve, or that it used to be farmland, but in fact it was industrial land for nearly fifty years.

lines.en: We get around forty thousand visitors a year. Most people come at weekends, of course, and summer is busy, but our busiest time is actually the spring school holidays, when the young birds hatch.

Now, what will you be doing? Many of you told me you'd like to work outdoors, on the reserve itself. That will come, but for the first month all new volunteers work in the visitor centre, helping at the information desk. That way you get to know the site and the people who visit it.

On the subject of guided walks: we used to run them every day, but we found that many visitors preferred to explore on their own, so now we only run them on Sunday mornings. They're very popular, so booking is essential.

One thing I must stress is safety. The paths are generally easy, but the boardwalks over the water can be slippery after rain. And the most important rule of all: please make sure visitors never feed the birds bread. It's bad for them, and it pollutes the water. If people ask, we sell proper bird food in the shop.

Right, let me tell you about some of the areas of the reserve. The first place most visitors head for is the Reed Bed Hide. A hide, if you don't know, is a small building where you can watch wildlife without being seen. This one is especially good for spotting otters. We've seen them there at least once a week this year.
Next is the Meadow. In early summer it's full of wild flowers, and it's the best place on the site to see butterflies.

Then there's the Children's Discovery Zone. This includes a pond-dipping area, where children use nets to look at the creatures living in the water. Sessions start every half hour and last about 20 minutes.
lines.say: Then there's the Children's Discovery Zone. This includes a pond-dipping area, where children use nets to look at the creatures living in the water. Sessions start every half hour and last about twenty minutes.

lines.en: Over on the east side is the Lookout Tower. It's 12 metres high, and from the top you can see right across the reserve. Unfortunately there's no lift, so it isn't suitable for wheelchair users.
lines.say: Over on the east side is the Lookout Tower. It's twelve metres high, and from the top you can see right across the reserve. Unfortunately there's no lift, so it isn't suitable for wheelchair users.

lines.en: And finally, the café. It's just been completely renovated, and it now has a terrace overlooking the main lake, which I'm sure will be very popular once the weather warms up.

parts.title: A research project on urban beekeeping
parts.context_zh: 第三部分：两个学生（Maya 和 Ben）和导师讨论城市养蜂的调查项目

lines.en: Come in, Maya, Ben. So, how's the beekeeping project going?
Pretty well, I think. We've finished the survey and most of the interviews.
Good. Remind me why you chose this topic. Was it because of your uncle, Ben? You mentioned he keeps bees.
He does, but that wasn't really the reason. I'd never been that interested, to be honest.
What actually got us started was a news report saying that the number of beehives in London had more than doubled in ten years. We wondered who all these new beekeepers were.
Fair enough. And how did the questionnaire go?

We got more responses than we expected, about eighty. The problem was that quite a few people misunderstood one of the questions. We asked how many hives they had, and some people counted the boxes inside each hive instead.

That happens. Make sure you explain how you dealt with it in the methodology section. Now, I've read your draft. The literature review is a reasonable length, but most of your sources are more than ten years old. You really need to include more recent studies.
OK, we'll look for some.
What did you find about the beekeepers themselves?
That was the surprising part. We expected most of them to be people who'd kept bees for decades, but in fact the majority had started in the last five years.
And fewer than half of them belonged to a beekeeping club, which was also unexpected.
Interesting. So what are your next steps?
I'm going to redo the charts. They're a bit hard to read at the moment.
And I'll contact the local council. We want to find out whether there are any rules about keeping bees in gardens.
Good. Now, let's talk about the presentation next week. You've got five sections. What are you planning to do with the introduction?
We think it's too long at the moment, so we'll make it shorter. We'll keep the main points, though.
And the section on the history of beekeeping?
Honestly, it isn't really relevant to our research question, so we've decided to drop it completely.
I agree. What about the survey results?
At the moment it's just numbers. We're going to add some photos of the hives we visited, so people can picture what we're talking about.
Good idea. And the interviews?
We were going to cut some of the quotations, but we've decided they work well as they are. We won't change that section.
And finally, the problems you faced?
We've got that near the beginning, but it would make more sense to discuss it after the results. So we'll move it to the end.
That sounds like a sensible plan.

parts.title: The development of the bicycle
parts.context_zh: 第四部分：一场关于自行车发展史的讲座

lines.en: Today I'm going to talk about the bicycle, a machine that most of us take for granted, but which had a surprisingly large effect on society.

The story usually begins in 1817, with a German inventor called Karl von Drais. His machine had two wheels and could be steered, but it had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet, rather like a child's balance bike today.
lines.say: The story usually begins in eighteen seventeen, with a German inventor called Karl von Drais. His machine had two wheels and could be steered, but it had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet, rather like a child's balance bike today.

lines.en: In the 1860s, pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, creating what was called the velocipede. In Britain, people gave it a less flattering name: the boneshaker. With iron tyres on rough or cobbled roads, you can imagine why.
lines.say: In the eighteen sixties, pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, creating what was called the velocipede. In Britain, people gave it a less flattering name: the boneshaker. With iron tyres on rough or cobbled roads, you can imagine why.

lines.en: Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, the bigger that wheel was, the further the bicycle travelled with each turn. So in the 1870s, designers made the front wheel larger and larger, producing the high-wheeler, which gave riders much greater speed. The problem was that the rider sat so high that any obstacle could send them flying over the handlebars, and serious falls were common.
lines.say: Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, the bigger that wheel was, the further the bicycle travelled with each turn. So in the eighteen seventies, designers made the front wheel larger and larger, producing the high-wheeler, which gave riders much greater speed. The problem was that the rider sat so high that any obstacle could send them flying over the handlebars, and serious falls were common.

lines.en: The solution came in 1885 with the Rover, often called the first safety bicycle. Its two wheels were roughly the same size, and the pedals drove the back wheel by means of a chain. Riders could now go fast without sitting dangerously high.
lines.say: The solution came in eighteen eighty-five with the Rover, often called the first safety bicycle. Its two wheels were roughly the same size, and the pedals drove the back wheel by means of a chain. Riders could now go fast without sitting dangerously high.

lines.en: Three years later, in 1888, John Boyd Dunlop developed an air-filled tyre. Interestingly, he wasn't thinking about bicycles at all: he wanted to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. But the air-filled tyre made cycling far smoother, and within a few years it was standard.
lines.say: Three years later, in eighteen eighty-eight, John Boyd Dunlop developed an air-filled tyre. Interestingly, he wasn't thinking about bicycles at all: he wanted to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. But the air-filled tyre made cycling far smoother, and within a few years it was standard.

lines.en: So what were the social effects? First, the bicycle gave ordinary people a cheap way to travel. A bicycle cost far less than keeping a horse, which needed feeding and stabling every day.
This had an impact on where people lived. Workers no longer had to live within walking distance of their workplace, so towns began to spread outwards.
The bicycle was also important for women. It gave them a new kind of independence, and it led to changes in clothing, as long, heavy skirts were simply impractical on a bicycle.

Cyclists also became an organised group with political influence. In both Britain and the United States, they campaigned for better road surfaces, years before cars became common. In a sense, the smooth roads that motorists later enjoyed were first demanded by cyclists.
And today, of course, many cities are encouraging cycling again. Pollution is often mentioned, but the main reason given by most city governments is to reduce congestion.

parts.title: Booking a holiday cottage
parts.context_zh: 第一部分：一位男士打电话预订海边度假小屋

lines.en: Good afternoon, Seaview Holiday Cottages. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a cottage for a week in August, if you've got anything available.
Let me have a look. Which week were you thinking of?
We'd like to arrive on Saturday the 9th and leave on the 16th.
lines.say: We'd like to arrive on Saturday the ninth and leave on the sixteenth.

lines.en: Yes, we've still got a few cottages free that week. How many people is it for?
There are five of us: two adults and three children.
OK. Rock Cottage is lovely, but it only sleeps four, so that would be too small. Gull Cottage sleeps six, and it's just a five-minute walk from the beach.
Gull Cottage sounds perfect. How much is it for the week?
In August it's 840 pounds for the week.
lines.say: In August it's eight hundred and forty pounds for the week.

lines.en: And do you need a deposit?
Yes, we ask for a deposit of 200 pounds when you book, and the rest four weeks before you arrive.
lines.say: Yes, we ask for a deposit of two hundred pounds when you book, and the rest four weeks before you arrive.

lines.en: Fine. Is bed linen included?
Bed linen is included, but towels aren't. You can hire them for five pounds per person, or bring your own.
We'll bring our own. Oh, and we've got a dog. Is that allowed?
Dogs are welcome in Gull Cottage, but there's an extra charge of 25 pounds for cleaning.
lines.say: Dogs are welcome in Gull Cottage, but there's an extra charge of twenty-five pounds for cleaning.

lines.en: That's fine.
Lovely. Can I take your name?
Yes, it's Martin Fenwick. That's F-E-N-W-I-C-K.
lines.say: Yes, it's Martin Fenwick. That's F. E. N. W. I. C. K.

lines.en: Thank you, Mr Fenwick. And what time do you expect to arrive on the Saturday? Check-in is from four o'clock.
It's a long drive, so we'll probably get there at about six.
That's no problem. Nobody will be there to meet you, but the key will be in a key safe by the front door. I'll text you the code on the morning you arrive.
Great. And is there parking at the cottage?
There's space for one car outside. If you've got a second car, there's a public car park by the harbour.
We'll only have one car. Lastly, is there anywhere to buy food nearby?
There's a small supermarket in the village, but it closes at eight, so you might want to bring some shopping with you for the first evening.
Good to know. Thanks very much.

parts.title: A food festival
parts.context_zh: 第二部分：本地电台介绍周末的美食节

lines.en: Good morning, and welcome to Weekend Live. If you're looking for something to do this weekend, the Millbrook Food Festival is back for its twelfth year, and I've got all the details for you.

The festival runs from Friday to Sunday in Victoria Park. In previous years it was held in the market square, but it's grown so much that the organisers have had to move it. Entry is free, as always, though some of the cookery classes do have a small charge.
This year the organisers have chosen a theme. Last year it was all about cheese, and next year they're thinking of focusing on bread, but this year it's fish and seafood.
There'll be around sixty stalls, and what the organisers are most proud of is that more than half of them are run by producers from within twenty miles of the town.
Getting there: parking near the park is very limited, so the organisers are strongly encouraging people to use the free shuttle bus from the railway station, which runs every fifteen minutes.

And a request from the organisers. Last year a lot of rubbish was left behind, so this year all food will be served on plates that can be composted, and visitors are asked to bring their own cups for drinks.
Now, let me run through some of the highlights. On Friday evening the festival opens with a street food market, which goes on until ten.
If you're interested in learning to cook, the fish cookery class with local chef Anna Price is on Saturday morning. It's already very popular, so book early.
Children haven't been forgotten. There's a cake-decorating competition for under-twelves, and that's on Sunday afternoon.
On Saturday evening there's live music on the main stage, with three local bands.
And finally, the oyster-opening championship, which always draws a big crowd, has moved this year from Saturday to Sunday morning. So that's the Millbrook Food Festival. Enjoy your weekend!

items.at: The festival runs from Friday to Sunday in Victoria Park

parts.title: Planning a project on sleep

lines.en: Hi Raj. Shall we sort out the plan for our sleep project?
Sure. Did you get a chance to look at the reading list Dr Mills gave us?

I read most of it. The article I found most useful was the one about screen use before bed. The one on caffeine was interesting, but it was mostly about older adults, so I'm not sure how relevant it is to students.
OK. So what should our main question be? I was thinking we could look at whether students who sleep less get lower marks.
That would be interesting, but we'd never get access to people's marks. They're confidential. What about comparing how much students sleep during term and during the holidays?
Good idea. That's something people can actually tell us.
How should we collect the data? An online questionnaire is the obvious choice.
Yes, but people tend to guess when you ask them how long they slept. It would be more accurate to ask a small group to keep a sleep diary for two weeks.
That's a lot more work for them, though. Maybe we could do both: the diary with a small group and the questionnaire for everyone else.
Let's do that.
How many people do we need for the questionnaire? Dr Mills said at least fifty.
Let's aim for a hundred. Then we'll still have enough even if some answers are incomplete.
Right. And when should we finish collecting data? The report's due at the end of March.
We'll need time to analyse everything, so let's finish by the end of February.
OK, let's divide up the jobs. I'm happy to write the questionnaire, since I did one last term.
Great. Then I'll find people for the sleep diary. I know a lot of people in my hall of residence.
What about the ethics form? Doesn't that need both of us?
Yes, it has to be completed and signed by both of us. Let's do it together on Friday.
And the data analysis? I'm not great with statistics.
I don't mind doing that. I quite enjoy it, actually.
Thanks. In that case I'll make the slides for the presentation.
Perfect. And we can share the writing of the final report.

parts.title: How habits form
parts.context_zh: 第四部分：一场关于习惯如何形成的讲座

lines.en: In today's lecture I want to look at habits: what they are, how they form, and why they're so hard to change.

Psychologists generally define a habit as a behaviour that is triggered automatically by a particular situation, without much conscious thought. And a surprisingly large part of our everyday behaviour is habitual. One well-known study found that around forty per cent of the things people did each day were repeated in the same place almost every day.

A useful way to think about a habit is as a loop with three parts. First, there's a cue: something in the environment, such as a time of day, a place, or a feeling. Then there's the routine, which is the behaviour itself. And finally there's a reward, which makes the behaviour more likely to be repeated the next time the cue appears.

You may have heard that it takes twenty-one days to form a new habit. In fact, that figure doesn't come from any scientific study. When researchers in London asked volunteers to adopt a new daily behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water with breakfast, they found that it took an average of 66 days for the behaviour to become automatic.
lines.say: You may have heard that it takes twenty-one days to form a new habit. In fact, that figure doesn't come from any scientific study. When researchers in London asked volunteers to adopt a new daily behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water with breakfast, they found that it took an average of sixty-six days for the behaviour to become automatic.

lines.en: There was also enormous variation. For some people it took as little as eighteen days; for others, more than eight months. Interestingly, missing a single day didn't seem to make much difference. What mattered was consistency over time.

So how can we use this knowledge? One effective strategy is to link a new habit to an existing one. For example, you might do two minutes of stretching straight after brushing your teeth. The existing habit acts as the cue.
Another strategy is to make the behaviour you want as easy as possible. If you want to go running in the morning, put your running shoes by the bed the night before.

Breaking a bad habit is harder, because the cue keeps appearing. Simply trying to resist through willpower usually fails. It's generally more effective to change the environment so that the cue doesn't occur, or, if that isn't possible, to replace the old routine with a new one that gives a similar reward. For instance, someone who always reaches for a snack when they feel bored might go for a short walk instead.

parts.title: Millbrook Community Garden
parts.context_zh: 第二部分：社区花园的负责人给新志愿者介绍花园

lines.en: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook Community Garden. My name's Tom, and I coordinate the volunteers here. Before we start work, I'd like to tell you a little about the garden and show you around.

The garden opened eight years ago on land that used to be a car park. The council originally planned to build flats here, but local residents campaigned to turn it into a garden instead, and in the end the council agreed to lease the land to us for a small fee.

Today we have about sixty regular volunteers. Most of them live within walking distance, but quite a few come from the other side of the city, which always surprises visitors. What brings them here, they tell us, isn't really the vegetables. It's the chance to meet people.

We grow food, of course, and most of it goes to a local food bank. We used to sell some of it at a weekly market, but we stopped doing that last year because it took up too much of the volunteers' time.

A few safety points. Please wear gloves when you're working with the compost, and wash your hands before you eat. The tools are kept in the shed, and we ask you to clean them before you put them back. If you see anything broken, tell me rather than trying to repair it yourself.

Right, let me tell you about the different areas, so you know where you'll be working. As you come in through the main gate, the first thing you'll see on your left is the herb garden. That's where we grow plants for cooking, and also some that attract bees.
Next to the herb garden is the greenhouse. At this time of year it's full of tomato plants, and it's also where we raise young plants before they go outside.

Behind the greenhouse, in the far corner, there's the pond. It was dug by a group of schoolchildren three years ago, and it's now home to frogs and dragonflies. Please don't let children go near it without an adult.
In the middle of the garden are the raised beds. They're built at waist height, so that people who use wheelchairs or can't bend easily can garden comfortably.
On the right-hand side is the orchard, with about twenty apple and pear trees. In the autumn we hold a harvest party there, and everyone's welcome to bring their families.

And finally, next to the main gate on the right, there's the kitchen, where we make tea, and where the cookery classes take place on Saturday mornings. Today you'll be working in the greenhouse and the raised beds. Shall we go?

parts.title: The history of street lighting
parts.context_zh: 第四部分：讲座——路灯的历史

lines.en: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about the history of street lighting, which is something most of us never think about, but which has changed the way cities work more than almost any other invention.

For most of history, city streets were completely dark at night. In medieval London, people who went out after dark were expected to carry their own light, and in many towns there were rules requiring householders to hang a lantern outside their door on winter evenings. These lanterns usually burned candles, and they gave very little light.

The first major change came with oil lamps in the seventeenth century. Paris introduced public lanterns in the 1660s, paid for by a special tax on residents. The lamps were lowered on ropes each evening so that they could be lit, and the men who did this job became a familiar sight.
lines.say: The first major change came with oil lamps in the seventeenth century. Paris introduced public lanterns in the sixteen-sixties, paid for by a special tax on residents. The lamps were lowered on ropes each evening so that they could be lit, and the men who did this job became a familiar sight.

lines.en: But the real revolution was gas. In 1807, Pall Mall in London became the first street in the world to be lit by gas. Gas lamps were far brighter than oil lamps, and within twenty years most large British cities had them. One of the most important effects was on crime. People felt safer walking at night, and shops could stay open later, which changed patterns of work and leisure.
lines.say: But the real revolution was gas. In eighteen-oh-seven, Pall Mall in London became the first street in the world to be lit by gas. Gas lamps were far brighter than oil lamps, and within twenty years most large British cities had them. One of the most important effects was on crime. People felt safer walking at night, and shops could stay open later, which changed patterns of work and leisure.

lines.en: Gas lighting also created a new job: the lamplighter. Every evening, lamplighters walked their routes with a long pole, turning on the gas and lighting each lamp, and every morning they returned to put them out. In some cities the lamplighter was also expected to act as a kind of watchman, reporting anything suspicious to the police.

Electric street lighting arrived in the 1870s, first using arc lamps, which were extremely bright but also noisy and expensive to maintain. It was only in the twentieth century, with the development of better bulbs, that electric lighting completely replaced gas. Interestingly, a few streets in London still have working gas lamps today, mainly for historical reasons.
lines.say: Electric street lighting arrived in the eighteen-seventies, first using arc lamps, which were extremely bright but also noisy and expensive to maintain. It was only in the twentieth century, with the development of better bulbs, that electric lighting completely replaced gas. Interestingly, a few streets in London still have working gas lamps today, mainly for historical reasons.

lines.en: In the last twenty years, cities have begun replacing older lights with LEDs. These use much less energy, and they can be dimmed late at night when the streets are empty. However, they have also caused concern. Many LEDs give off a cold blue light, which researchers believe can disturb the sleep of people living nearby and confuse insects and birds.

As a result, some cities now choose warmer colours for their street lights, and a few have introduced dark-sky zones, where lighting is reduced to protect wildlife and allow people to see the stars. So the history of street lighting may be turning full circle: after centuries of trying to make the night brighter, some cities are now deciding that a little darkness is worth keeping.

items.q: Oil lamps were lowered on ___ so they could be lit
items.at: The lamps were lowered on ropes each evening
items.why: 每晚用绳子把灯放下来点。

items.q: First gas-lit street: Pall ___ in London
items.at: Pall Mall in London became the first street
items.why: 伦敦的 Pall Mall 是世界上第一条煤气灯街道。

items.q: An important effect of gas lighting was on ___
items.at: One of the most important effects was on crime.
items.why: 煤气灯最重要的影响之一是减少犯罪，人们夜里更安心。

items.q: Lamplighters carried a long ___
items.at: lamplighters walked their routes with a long pole
items.why: 点灯人拿着长杆。

items.q: In some cities the lamplighter also acted as a ___
items.at: act as a kind of watchman
items.why: 兼当巡夜人，看到可疑情况报警。

items.q: Arc lamps were very bright but ___ and expensive
items.at: extremely bright but also noisy and expensive to maintain
items.why: 弧光灯很亮，但吵、维护贵。

items.q: LED lights can be ___ when streets are empty
items.at: they can be dimmed late at night when the streets are empty
items.why: 深夜街上没人时可以调暗。

items.q: Blue light may disturb people's ___
items.at: can disturb the sleep of people living nearby
items.why: 冷蓝光可能影响附近居民睡眠。
